title: SourceWrite · Core Intention and the Deletion Test

parts.title: Core Intention and Text Hierarchy
instruction: The first thing we will learn is that each text is intentional. By that we mean that the author of the text wants their audience to arrive somewhere: a specific action, or a new understanding, or a changed belief. The author’s intention is to make their audience do, feel, or think something.

But authors rarely state that intention by itself. They surround their intention with support which can be in the form of context, evidence, explanation, or examples. Our goal is to learn how to separate the core intention of the author from the supporting material that helps that intention succeed.

example.title: Store announcement
example.text: All shoppers please proceed to the checkout line at this time. This store is now closed. Thank you for shopping at Walmart!
example.explanation: Sentence 1: “All shoppers please proceed to the checkout line at this time,” because the core intention of the author is to encourage shoppers to go to checkout. Sentence 2 provides context and justification for the request, and sentence 3 is a politeness formula. They support the core intention.

parts.title: The Deletion Test
instruction: That instinct to scan for the most important information is exactly how strong readers tackle texts. But when texts get longer or trickier, intuition alone can sometimes lead us to the wrong sentence. We need a way to quickly spot the best sentence, and then prove that it is the right one.

To do this, we use the Deletion Test. This is a pairwise comparison: we look at what happens if we delete the rest of the text, versus what happens if we delete our candidate sentence. If we keep only the Main Sentence and delete everything else, the author's core intention will still survive. On the flip side, if we delete the Main Sentence and keep everything else, the core intention will be lost. This strategy works because the Main Sentence always carries the heaviest weight of the author's core intention.

example.title: Tornado warning
example.text: (1) This is a tornado warning. (2) Conditions outside have become dangerous. (3) Seek shelter in a sturdy building immediately. (4) Do not stop to take any belongings with you.
example.explanation: The instruction to seek shelter immediately communicates the core intention even without the other sentences.

practice.reason: This sentence best preserves the author’s central intention when the other sentences are removed.

parts.title: The Deletion Test for Paragraphs
instruction: In the previous part, we used the Deletion Test to find the Main Sentence in a short text. We cut away all the supporting details to isolate the exact sentence that captured the author’s core intention.

But what happens when texts get longer? In college and your future career, you will rarely read just a single paragraph. You will read essays, reports, and articles. If you try to apply the Deletion Test to 50 sentences all at once, you will quickly get overwhelmed.

To tackle longer texts, we have to understand their structure. Longer texts are built in layers: they are organized into chapters, sections, and paragraphs. Today, we will apply the Deletion Test to longer essays by using the test twice:
first to find the most important paragraph,
and then to find the most important sentence inside it.

First, read or skim the whole text to get an overall sense of its structure and the author’s Core Intention: what the author wants us to do, think, or feel. This is our initial impression, not our final answer. As we examine the text more closely, we will use the Deletion Test to check whether our initial understanding is correct.

example.title: High school start times
example.text:
High schools should begin the school day later because students learn more effectively when they get enough sleep. Many teenagers do not naturally become tired early in the evening, which makes it difficult for them to get the recommended amount of rest before early morning classes. When students arrive at school exhausted, they may struggle to focus, participate, and remember important information. A later start time would create conditions that help students be healthier and more successful learners.

One reason schools should start later is that additional sleep can improve students’ ability to concentrate in class. When students are well rested, they are more prepared to listen, solve problems, and complete challenging assignments. In contrast, students who begin the day while still tired may have difficulty paying attention or staying motivated. By allowing students more time to sleep, schools can help create classrooms where students are ready to learn.

A later start time can also improve students’ overall well-being. Teenagers often balance schoolwork with activities, jobs, and family responsibilities, leaving them with limited time for sleep. When students consistently miss sleep, they may experience increased stress and have less energy throughout the day. Starting school later would give students a better opportunity to maintain a healthy routine, which can support both academic achievement and personal health.
example.explanation: The first paragraph establishes the overall argument; its first sentence states the central claim.

practice.title: Practice Item 9 — Original Handout 3, Text 2
paragraphs: College students often face challenges when trying to maintain healthy routines while balancing classes, assignments, and other responsibilities. Many universities provide fitness centers and optional wellness programs, but these opportunities depend on students choosing to participate. Because of these challenges, colleges continue to explore ways to support students’ overall well-being.

Regular exercise can provide many benefits for college students, including improved energy, reduced stress, and better daily routines. However, these benefits are not always experienced by students who do not participate in optional fitness programs. Colleges should require all students to complete a physical education class because exercise is an essential part of a complete education. A required gym course would give every student the opportunity to learn how to maintain an active lifestyle and develop healthy habits that can continue after graduation.

Some people argue that college students should be responsible for choosing whether they exercise. They believe universities should focus only on traditional academic subjects. However, colleges already require courses that develop skills students will use throughout their lives, such as writing and communication. Physical education deserves similar attention because maintaining good health can help students succeed both during college and beyond.
practice.reason: The main paragraph expresses the overall claim; the selected sentence most directly communicates that claim.

practice.title: Practice Item 10 — Original Handout 3, Text 3
paragraphs: Many college courses include individual assignments, exams, and projects that require students to work independently. Individual work can help students develop personal responsibility and allow instructors to evaluate each student’s understanding. However, students in the workplace and in many professional environments are often expected to collaborate with others. Because of this, colleges must consider how their assignments prepare students for future situations.

Students may encounter group activities in a variety of college courses, such as presentations, research projects, and classroom discussions. These activities often require students to communicate with classmates, organize their responsibilities, and complete tasks together. While these experiences are common in higher education, they are not always designed in a way that helps students fully develop their teamwork abilities.

Although some students dislike group projects because of unequal participation, well-designed group assignments can provide valuable learning experiences. Students can learn how to divide responsibilities, manage disagreements, and support their teammates when challenges arise. These skills are difficult to develop through individual assignments alone because they require students to interact with others and work toward a shared goal. It is therefore clear that increasing opportunities for group work is how colleges can successfully equip students with the essential communication and teamwork skills they need for success beyond the classroom.
practice.reason: The main paragraph expresses the overall claim; the selected sentence most directly communicates that claim.

test.question: What is the “core intention” of a text?
options: A. The very first sentence of the paragraph.
B. The background information that explains why the text was written.
C. The action, thought, or feeling the author wants the audience to walk away with.
D. The polite greetings and sign-offs at the beginning and end of a message.

test.question: What does it mean when we say a text has a “hierarchy”?
options: A. Not all sentences carry the same amount of weight.
B. Every text should be organized using bullet points and numbered lists.
C. Shorter sentences are always more important than longer sentences.
D. A text must always be read slowly, word-for-word, from beginning to end.

test.question: When we use the Deletion Test, what are we trying to figure out?
options: A. How many sentences we can cut to make the text shorter.
B. Which sentence is the longest and most descriptive.
C. If a single sentence can successfully deliver the author's core intention on its own.
D. Which sentence uses the most difficult vocabulary.

test.question: Use the Deletion Test to identify the main sentence (Text A).
sentences: The museum has displayed many important historical artifacts over the years.
Please return all borrowed exhibit materials to the information desk before leaving the museum today.
We appreciate your help in protecting these valuable items.

test.question: Use the Deletion Test to identify the main sentence (Text B).
sentences: Maria practiced her presentation several times before the competition.
She reviewed her notes, adjusted her slides, and asked her classmates for feedback.
When she presented, the judges selected her project as the winning presentation.
Her classmates congratulated her afterward.

test.question: Why do we identify the Main Paragraph before identifying the Main Sentence?
options: A. The Main Sentence is always located in the paragraph with the most details.
B. The Main Paragraph contains every important fact in the text.
C. The Main Paragraph is the paragraph that best communicates the author’s core intention.
D. Supporting paragraphs are unnecessary once the Main Paragraph is found.

test.question: Select the main paragraph and then its main sentence (Text A).
paragraphs: Many schools have created programs that allow students to participate in community service projects during the year. These projects often involve activities such as helping local organizations or supporting neighborhood events.

For many students, community service opportunities help develop responsibility while strengthening their connection to the community. These experiences also build leadership, communication, and problem-solving skills beyond the classroom.
Some students volunteer at food banks or community centers during weekends. Others help organize donation drives or participate in environmental clean-up projects.

test.question: Select the main paragraph and then its main sentence (Text B).
paragraphs: Technology has changed the way many students complete assignments and communicate with teachers. Digital tools are now common in classrooms and are used for research, collaboration, and organization.
Some students believe technology can sometimes create distractions during learning. Others argue that students need guidance to use digital tools effectively and responsibly.

Teaching students to use technology responsibly prepares them for academic success and future careers. Learning to evaluate information and communicate online helps students meet challenges beyond the classroom.
